meta.blurb: Every year a pearl arrives in the post for Mary Morstan, and no one will say who sends it. Her father vanished long ago. Holmes and Watson follow a clever little dog and a fast boat after a stolen fortune.
meta.bible: Sherlock Holmes: the consulting detective, bored without a puzzle, brilliant, vain, kind underneath. Dr John Watson: his friend and the narrator, a doctor who falls in love. Miss Mary Morstan: a young governess whose father vanished in 1878; calm and brave. Captain Arthur Morstan: her father, an army officer from India. Major John Sholto: his friend, who came home with a hidden treasure. Thaddeus Sholto: the Major's nervous, kind son. Bartholomew Sholto: his twin brother, killed at Pondicherry Lodge. McMurdo: the old boxer who guards the gate. Mrs Bernstone: the housekeeper. Athelney Jones: the confident Scotland Yard inspector. Toby: a small ugly dog with a perfect nose. Mr Sherman: the man who lends Toby, of Pinchin Lane. Mordecai Smith: owner of the steam launch Aurora. Jim Smith: his son. Jonathan Small: a man with a wooden leg, the thief and prisoner. Tonga: Small's small friend from the Andaman Islands. Abdullah Khan, Mahomet Singh and Dost Akbar: the three Sikh soldiers who join Small. Achmet: the merchant killed at Agra. The sign of the four: the four names signed on the old plan. The Agra treasure: a hoard of jewels. London, Upper Norwood, Pondicherry Lodge, the Lyceum Theatre, Baker Street, the Thames, Agra, India, the Andaman Islands, Worcestershire. Voice and tone: lively, clever and atmospheric, with a mystery that unrolls clue by clue and a story of greed and revenge told by the villain; deaths are stated plainly, with no gore; the last pages are warm and a little sad. Beat 200 closes with Watson and Mary together and Holmes alone. Added for the full-length book: Mrs Cecil Forrester: Mary's kind employer, who sent her to Holmes. Wiggins: leader of the street boys, the Baker Street Irregulars, whom Holmes pays a shilling a day and a guinea for the boat. Wigmore Street: where Watson sent a telegram. Edinburgh: where Mary went to school. Pinchin Lane: where Mr Sherman lives with his birds and animals. Westminster Stairs: where the police launch waits. Port Blair: the convict station on the Andaman Islands. Pershore: the Worcestershire town near Small's family farm. The Ganges: the river where a crocodile took Small's leg. The Bay of Bengal. Afghanistan: where Watson was wounded. Euclid: the geometer Holmes mentions. Gregson and Lestrade: Scotland Yard detectives Holmes helps. The Times: the newspaper that carried the notice for Mary. Fixed facts: Captain Morstan vanished on 3 December 1878. Major Sholto died on 28 April 1882, and the first pearl came six days later. Mary has six pearls. Small guards a gate at the Agra fort in 1857 with the three Sikhs; Achmet is killed and the treasure buried; the four sign a plan with a cross. The four are sentenced to the Andamans. Small tells Sholto and Morstan of the treasure and gives Morstan the plan; Sholto keeps the whole treasure. Small escapes with Tonga in a canoe and later shows Tonga at fairs in England. The brothers find the treasure in a space above a ceiling at Pondicherry Lodge; Tonga enters through the roof by a rope. Small empties the iron box into the Thames before the chase. The chase ends when the Aurora runs onto a mudbank; Tonga is shot in the bow; Small's wooden leg sticks in the mud. Watson opens the empty box with a poker at Mrs Forrester's and tells Mary he loves her.

beats.scene: A small ship sails across a wide blue sea towards a green island
beats.summary: The four are shipped to the Andaman Islands, far across the sea.

beats.scene: Convicts in a bare clearing cut jungle under a burning sun
beats.summary: Prison life is hard, with heat, rain, fever and poor food.

beats.scene: A convict in a white apron carries bottles into a doctor's house
beats.summary: Small is given easier work at the doctor's house and learns a little medicine.

beats.scene: Two officers play cards on a lamplit veranda while a convict sweeps nearby
beats.summary: Major Sholto and Captain Morstan, who command the guard, play cards every evening.

beats.scene: A prisoner leans towards two officers at a card table
beats.summary: Small decides that this is his chance and offers to tell the officers about the treasure.

beats.scene: Small hands a folded yellowed paper to an officer in lamplight
beats.summary: The officers agree to share, and Small gives Captain Morstan the plan with the four names.

beats.scene: A ship sails away at dawn while a prisoner watches from a hill
beats.summary: Sholto goes to India, finds the treasure and keeps it all.

beats.scene: A prisoner reads a newspaper under a flickering lamp
beats.summary: Small learns that Sholto is a rich man in England and has cheated him.

beats.scene: Three Sikh prisoners sit together, talking in low voices, in a bare yard
beats.summary: His three Sikh friends are as angry as he is, but none can escape.

beats.scene: A man with a wooden leg stares out to sea from a high rock
beats.summary: Year after year Small watches the sea and waits for a chance to escape.

beats.scene: A small dark man lies hurt among the reeds of a swamp
beats.summary: Small finds a little islander, sick and hurt and alone, in the swamp.

beats.scene: A small man smiles and drinks from a cup while a bigger man watches
beats.summary: Tonga recovers and becomes Small's devoted friend.

beats.scene: Tonga paddles a long thin canoe through a quiet bay at sunset
beats.summary: Tonga has a canoe and knows all the waters of the islands.

beats.scene: Two men whisper together in a dark hut, planning
beats.summary: Small tells Tonga his plan and they choose a dark, stormy night.

beats.scene: A canoe slips out over black water under a stormy sky
beats.summary: They slip away in the canoe on a wild night.

beats.scene: A small canoe floats on a calm empty sea under a hot sun
beats.summary: They drift for days at sea until a ship picks them up.

beats.scene: Crowds watch a small man in island dress dance on a fairground stage
beats.summary: In England they live by earning pennies at fairs, where Tonga dances in island dress.

beats.scene: A man with a wooden leg reads a newspaper under a street lamp
beats.summary: Small learns that Sholto lives at Upper Norwood and is in poor health.

beats.scene: A bearded face looks in through a window at a dying man
beats.summary: Small looks through the Major's window, and the Major sees him, screams and dies.

beats.scene: Small searches a dead man's room by lamplight and writes a note
beats.summary: Small returns later, searches the room, finds nothing and leaves the sign of the four.

beats.scene: A man waits in a foggy lane beside a high garden wall
beats.summary: For six years Small and Tonga wait in London, until word comes that the treasure is found.

beats.scene: Two figures and a coil of rope stand beside a high garden wall
beats.summary: Small and Tonga go to Pondicherry Lodge, and Tonga climbs a rope to the roof.

beats.scene: A small figure drops through a hole in a ceiling into a lamplit room
beats.summary: Tonga drops through the ceiling, and Bartholomew sees him.

beats.scene: A small man blows through a pipe at a man in a chair
beats.summary: Tonga, in sudden rage, shoots Bartholomew with a poisoned dart, which Small never wished.

beats.scene: A box is lowered on a rope from a roof to a waiting man
beats.summary: Tonga leaves the note, lowers the iron box by the rope and slides down after it.

beats.scene: A dark launch with a tall funnel moves down a river at night
beats.summary: They carry the box to the Aurora, hired from Mordecai Smith, and hide on the river.

beats.scene: A man tips jewels from an iron box into a dark river
beats.summary: Small says that, if he could not have the treasure, nobody should, so he emptied the box into the river.

beats.scene: Small sits back with a cold cigar as Jones leads him away
beats.summary: Small says that he never meant Bartholomew harm and grieves for Tonga, and Jones leads him away.

beats.scene: Holmes smiles dryly at Watson across a table in the early light
beats.summary: Holmes congratulates Watson in his dry way and says that he will never marry.

beats.scene: Holmes stands alone at the window of Baker Street in the rain
beats.summary: Jones gets the credit, Watson goes to his new life, and Holmes waits alone for the next puzzle.

A1A2: Holmes was bored, so he took down his small bottle.
Watson was a doctor, and he begged Holmes to put it away.
Holmes said that he was the only detective of his kind.
Holmes said that Watson's little book had too much romance.
Holmes saw mud on Watson's shoe and knew where he had been.
Watson gave Holmes an old watch and asked him to look at it.
Holmes looked closely at the watch, and then he opened it.
Holmes said that the owner was careless and drank too much.
Watson was angry, but Holmes said that he was truly sorry.
Just then someone knocked, and the maid said that a lady was waiting.
A young woman in a plain grey dress came into the room.
Mary said that she was a teacher and needed their advice.
Her father was an army officer, and he worked in far-off India.
In 1878 her father came home, and she hurried to meet him.
She asked the police, and she put notices in the newspapers.
Then, in 1882, a notice in the newspaper asked for her address.
Inside the box there was one large and very beautiful pearl.
This morning, a new letter told her to meet a friend.
She showed them an old paper that had been her father's.
Four names were written on the back, with four little crosses.
Mary promised to come back at half past six, and left.
Watson said that she was lovely, but Holmes had not noticed.
Holmes said that a charming woman can also be a wicked one.
Holmes took the paper and went out to look up some facts.
Watson tried to read, but he could only think of Mary.
Holmes learned that Major Sholto died six days before the first pearl.
At half past six Mary came, and they all left together.
They waited by the third pillar, and the crowd hurried past.
A small man spoke to Mary and asked about her friends.
He whistled for a cab, and the three of them got in.
Holmes named each street as they drove through the city.
Then the fog got thicker, and Holmes did not know the way.
The cab stopped at last, and a servant opened the door.
Inside, the house was full of beautiful and costly things.
A small bald man stood up, and his hands were shaking.
He asked Watson to listen to his heart, and it was fine.
He said her father was dead, and Mary turned very white.
Thaddeus began the story of his father, Major Sholto.
The Major was afraid of any man with a wooden leg.
Captain Morstan came to see him, and then he died.
The Major hid the body and told nobody about it.
In 1882 the old Major was ill, and he called his sons.
He said that he wanted to tell them a great secret.
Suddenly he saw a face at the window and screamed.
That night the Major died, and they found a strange note.
For six years the brothers looked for the treasure.
Thaddeus sent Mary a pearl each year, so she was not poor.
At last Bartholomew found the treasure inside the house.
They saw a huge pile of jewels, and Thaddeus thought of Mary.
Then Thaddeus took them in a carriage to his brother's house.
They drove for a long time through the dark fog.
The house was behind a high wall and a heavy gate.
A huge old fighter named McMurdo stood at the gate.
Holmes said they had boxed once, and McMurdo laughed.
Holmes laughed softly, and the old man opened the gate.
The garden was full of deep holes and heaps of earth.
The housekeeper met them and said that she was afraid.
Mrs Bernstone took Mary away, and the men went upstairs.
Thaddeus looked into the lock, and he screamed in fear.
Holmes and Watson pushed hard and broke down the door.
A dead man sat in a chair, and his face looked strange.
The window was shut, and the key was inside the door.
Watson felt the man's wrist, but he was already dead.
Watson found a long dark thorn in the man's head.
Holmes said that the thorn had a poison on it.
On the table was a note with four strange words.
Thaddeus was afraid that the police would blame him.
Watson went downstairs and told Mary the sad news.
Holmes searched the whole room with great care.
Holmes saw a hole in the ceiling and climbed up.
Holmes found small footprints in the dust above the room.
Holmes smelled a strong tar smell on the small footprints.
Holmes said that a second man must have helped him.
In the garden, Holmes found the mark of a wooden leg.
Inspector Jones came, and he was loud and very sure of himself.
Jones took Thaddeus away, but Holmes said that he was wrong.
Holmes told Jones about the two men he was looking for.
Watson took Mary home in a cab, and they were quiet.
Mary thanked Watson, and he walked away deep in thought.
Holmes read about small island people with poison darts.
At dawn, Holmes and Watson went to Pinchin Lane.
A man shouted angrily from a window above the door.
Inside, there were many cages and stuffed birds everywhere.
Sherman brought out Toby, a funny little brown and white dog.
Holmes paid some money, and Sherman gave him the dog.
They took Toby in a cab back to the big house.
Toby smelled the footprints, and then he ran off quickly.
They followed Toby along the streets as the sun rose.
Watson doubted the dog, but Holmes believed in his nose.
Toby ran into a yard full of tall piles of wood.
Toby ran to a big barrel, and he sat down there.
Holmes said that Toby had gone the wrong way.
Holmes called Toby back and tried to find the other trail.
Toby ran between tall buildings towards the river.
The trail ended at the water, so they had taken a boat.
A worried woman came out of a small house nearby.
She said her husband had a fast boat called Aurora.
Her husband had taken the boat out, and he was late.
Holmes said that they must find the Aurora quickly.
They took Toby home and went back to Baker Street.
Watson woke up, and Holmes was making a plan.
A dozen ragged boys ran into the sitting room together.
Holmes told them to look for a boat named Aurora.
Holmes promised a gold coin to the boy who found it.
Holmes dressed as an old sailor and went to the river.
Watson waited alone all day, but no news came.
An old sailor came in, and he was really Holmes.
Holmes said that he had learned nothing yet.
The newspapers wrote about the murder and praised Inspector Jones.
Wiggins came back, but he had no news about the boat.
Two days passed with no news, and Holmes was restless.
Watson went to see Mary and told her the news.
Mary said that money was not the most important thing.
Mrs Forrester asked Watson to visit again, and he said yes.
A boy ran in and said that he had found the boat.
Holmes sent for Jones, who came to Baker Street.
Jones said that he had been wrong about Thaddeus Sholto.
Watson took out his old army pistol and put it away.
A police boat was waiting for them at the river steps.
The launch went down the river as the evening grew dark.
The launch stopped in the shadows and put out its lights.
They waited in the cold and watched the dark yard.
Holmes warned Watson that the small man used poison darts.
A dark boat with a tall funnel came out of the yard.
Jones shouted for the boat to stop, but it did not.
The men put more coal on the fire and gave chase.
The Aurora was very fast, and the police could not catch her.
Watson saw a tall man steering, and a small shape in front.
Slowly the police boat was catching up with the Aurora.
Holmes and Watson raised their pistols as they came closer.
They both fired, and the small man cried out and fell.
They did not see the small man again that night.
The Aurora hit the mud and stopped hard.
The man with the wooden leg got stuck in the mud.
Holmes asked the man his name, and he said Jonathan Small.
In the cabin, the police found a heavy iron box.
Holmes said that Mary Morstan should see the box first.
They pulled both boats free and went back up the river.
Holmes said that the case was almost solved.
Watson looked at the iron box and thought of Mary.
Watson took the iron box to Mary in a cab.
Mary was waiting up, and she came to the door.
The box was locked, so Watson found a strong poker.
The box was open, but there was nothing inside.
Watson said, “Thank God,” and Mary was very surprised.
Watson told Mary that he loved her very much.
Mary smiled and said that she loved him too.
They sat together happily while the empty box stood nearby.
At last Watson left, but he promised to come back soon.
At Baker Street, Small agreed to tell his whole story.
Small said that he was born on a farm in England.
Small joined the army and went to India on a ship.
One hot day, Small went swimming in a wide river.
A crocodile took his leg, and a friend pulled him out.
In hospital, Small learned that he could not be a soldier.
A kind planter gave him work on his big farm.
He was happy there, but then bad news came.
A great war began, and the whole country was on fire.
Small and the family hurried away to a strong fort.
At Agra, the fort was full of frightened people.
Small guarded a gate with three brave Sikh soldiers.
At night, the four men talked and became good friends.
One night, a rich man named Achmet came to the gate.
The man showed them jewels, and he asked for help.
The four men whispered, and they made a bad plan.
They killed the rich man before he could cry out.
They hid the body and the jewels in a quiet corner.
They drew a plan and wrote their four names on it.
At last, the English army won the war and the fighting ended.
The four men were caught and sent to prison on an island.
A ship took the four men far across the sea.
Life in the prison was hard, with heat and rain.
Small got an easier job at the doctor's house.
Two army officers played cards every evening, and Small listened.
Small decided to tell the officers about the treasure.
Small showed them the plan, and they agreed to help.
Sholto went to India and took the treasure for himself.
Small learned that Sholto had cheated him and was rich.
His three friends were angry too, but they could not leave.
Year after year, Small waited for a chance to escape.
Small found a little man who was ill and alone.
The little man got better, and he became Small's friend.
Tonga could paddle a canoe better than any other man.
Small and Tonga made a plan to escape at night.
In the dark, they got into the canoe and left.
They drifted for days at sea until a ship found them.
In England, they worked at fairs to make some money.
Small learned that Sholto lived in a house at Norwood.
Small looked through the window, and the Major screamed and died.
Small searched the room, but he found no treasure.
Small waited for years until he heard the treasure was found.
Tonga climbed a rope up to the roof of the house.
Tonga dropped into the room, and Bartholomew saw him.
Tonga shot a dart at the man, and he died.
Tonga lowered the box on a rope, and Small took it.
They took the box to the Aurora and went away.
Small threw the treasure into the river so nobody could have it.
Jones took Small away, and Small said that he had been robbed.
Holmes was glad for Watson, but he would never marry.
Watson went to his new life, and Holmes stood alone.
B1B2: It was a grey afternoon at Baker Street, and Holmes had no case and no visitor to occupy his mind. He took down his little bottle from the shelf, as he so often did when he was bored.
Watson, who was a doctor, asked him how long he meant to go on harming himself. Holmes only smiled and answered that his mind could not bear to be idle.

Holmes explained that he had invented his own profession, for he was the only consulting detective in the world. When the police or private people were lost, they came to him, and he put them on the right road.
Holmes picked up Watson's account of their first case and said that it was spoiled by romance. Detection, he said, ought to be an exact science, not a love story.
Holmes glanced at the red mud on Watson's shoe and said that he had been to the post office in Wigmore Street. He added that Watson had sent a telegram there, not a letter.
Watson smiled, because he thought that he could now test his friend. He gave Holmes an old watch that had just come to him and asked what he could learn about its last owner.
Holmes opened the back of the watch and studied the inside with his glass. He found fine scratches round the keyhole, and he found numbers that pawnbrokers had scratched inside the case.
Holmes said that the watch had belonged to Watson's elder brother, who had been careless, lazy and fond of drink. He had started life with good prospects, but he had wasted them and had died poor.

Watson cried that Holmes must have spied on his poor brother's life, and he walked angrily across the room. Holmes said that he had not even known that Watson had a brother, and that he was truly sorry.
Holmes said that it was only a matter of small signs, and that Watson must forgive him. Just then someone knocked, and the maid said that a young lady wished to see Mr Holmes.
She was neatly dressed in plain grey, with a quiet face and large, kind blue eyes. Watson thought that he had never seen a lady so gentle and so calm.

She introduced herself as Miss Mary Morstan and said that she worked as a governess in the house of a Mrs Forrester. Mrs Forrester had once been helped by Holmes, and she had kindly advised Mary to come to him.
Her mother had died long ago, and her father, Captain Morstan, had been an army officer in India for many years. She had grown up at a boarding school in Edinburgh, and she had seen him only seldom.
In December 1878 her father telegraphed that he had reached London on leave, and she hurried to meet him. At his hotel the clerk said that he had gone out the night before and had not come back.
She went to the police and put advertisements in the newspapers, but no word of him ever came. His only friend in London was Major Sholto, who said that he had never known of Morstan's return.
In May 1882 a notice in The Times asked for the address of Miss Mary Morstan. She sent it, and a small box arrived by post.
Inside the box lay one very large pearl, but there was no letter to say who had sent it. A new box has come on the same day every year since, and she now has six pearls.

That morning she had received a letter telling her to wait at the third pillar of the Lyceum Theatre at seven o'clock. It promised her justice, and it said that she might bring two friends but no police.

She also showed them an old paper that she had found among her father's belongings, and Holmes spread it out on the table. It was a rough plan of a large building, with a small red cross in one corner.

On the back of the plan four names were written in ink, and beneath them were the words “the sign of the four.” Holmes said nothing for a long while, and then he asked if he might keep the paper until the evening.
Mary promised to come back at half-past six and then walked away down Baker Street. Watson went to the window and watched her until she was lost in the crowd.
Watson cried that she was a most attractive woman, but Holmes said coolly that he had not noticed. A client, he explained, was only a unit in a problem, and feelings spoiled clear thought.
Holmes said that the most charming woman he had ever known had been hanged for a terrible crime. Watson was shocked, but he knew that Holmes liked to speak in this cold way.
Holmes folded the old paper into his pocket-book and said that he must find some dates in the records. He told Watson to be back by half-past six, and then he went out into the street.
Watson went back to his own rooms and tried to read, but the words ran together before his eyes. He kept seeing Mary's quiet face and thinking of her lost father and the strange pearls.

Holmes came back with his notes and told Watson that Major Sholto had died on the twenty-eighth of April 1882. The first pearl had arrived only six days later, and Holmes did not think that this was chance.
Holmes thought that the Major's heir might be trying to put right an old wrong. At half-past six Mary arrived, calm and pale, and the three of them set off for the Lyceum in a cab.
At seven o'clock they stood by the third pillar outside the Lyceum, while a stream of people hurried past. Mary was pale and silent, and Watson watched every stranger who came near.
A small, rough man in a coachman's coat touched Mary's arm and asked if she had come with two friends. He also wanted to be sure that neither of them was a policeman.
The man whistled, and a closed cab rattled up to the pavement. He opened the door, waited for them to climb in, and then jumped up beside the driver as the horses started.

Holmes called out the names of the streets as they passed, Rochester Row, Vincent Square and then the Vauxhall Bridge Road. Soon they crossed the river by the bridge, and he said that they were making for the south side of London.
Soon the fog grew thicker, and the lamps became yellow smudges in the gloom. Even Holmes said that he had lost the way, and nobody spoke while the cab rolled on.
At last the cab stopped outside a plain, ugly house in a dark and poorly lit street. Before they could knock, the door opened, and a servant in a yellow turban and white clothes stood in the light.
The poor, dark outside of the house had not prepared them for the rooms inside. Heavy carpets, silk curtains, costly pictures and Eastern vases stood everywhere, like jewels set in a plain frame.
In the middle of this splendour stood a small man with a high, bald head and a few strands of red hair. His hands twitched all the time, and his lips shook as he spoke.
Thaddeus begged Watson, as a medical man, to listen to his heart, because he feared that it was weak. Watson found nothing wrong with it, and the little man was greatly relieved.
Thaddeus said gently that he knew what had happened to her father, and that he was no longer alive. Mary turned very white, but she said that she had feared it for years.
Thaddeus lit his hookah, leaned back among his cushions and began his story. His father, Major John Sholto, had once served in India with Captain Morstan, and he had returned to England a rich man.

The old Major was terribly afraid of men with wooden legs, and he never went out alone. Once he even fired a pistol at an innocent man with a wooden leg, and he had to pay money to keep the matter quiet.
In December 1878 Captain Morstan had come to Pondicherry Lodge to claim his share of a treasure. The two men quarrelled bitterly, and Morstan fell dead, struck down by a weak heart.
Thaddeus said that the Major had hidden the body and told nobody, because he was afraid that people would call him a murderer. From that day he was never at peace, and his health slowly failed.
In the spring of 1882 the old Major lay in bed and knew that he was dying. He sent for his twin sons, Thaddeus and Bartholomew, and asked them to sit beside him.
The old man told them about the treasure and about the death of Captain Morstan. He said that the jewels were hidden in the house, and he began to say where.
Suddenly the old man stared at the window and screamed that the man must be kept out. His sons turned and saw a wild, bearded face pressed against the glass, and then it was gone.
The Major fell back and died before he could say where the treasure was hidden. In the morning they found his room searched, and a paper on his chest bore the words “the sign of the four.”
For six years the two brothers searched the house and garden for the hidden jewels. Bartholomew had the whole garden dug up, but they found nothing, and they began to quarrel.
Thaddeus felt that Mary had been wronged, and he feared that she might be poor. Every year he sent her one of the few pearls that his father had left, because he dared not do more.

Only a short time ago Bartholomew measured the whole house and found that it was shorter inside than outside. He broke through a ceiling near the roof, and there, in a hidden space, lay the Agra treasure.
The two brothers looked at the heap of glittering jewels, which was worth a fortune. Thaddeus said that Mary Morstan must have a fair share, and he wanted to take her to his brother at once.
Thaddeus said that they must go to his brother's house together, and that they must go at once. He had a carriage ready, and they all set off for Upper Norwood.
They drove for many miles through the dark, and Thaddeus talked nervously all the way. He spoke of his pictures, his heart and his dislike of the police.
At last they stopped beside a high stone wall with a small iron-clamped door set in it. Thaddeus knocked in a curious way, and a deep, gruff voice answered from inside.
The door opened a little, and a huge man with a lantern looked out at them. This was McMurdo, an old boxer, who said that his master had given orders to let nobody in.

Holmes reminded him that they had boxed together some years before, on the night of his benefit. McMurdo stared, then laughed and said that he would have known him at once if he had thrown that cross-hit of his.
Holmes whispered to Watson that, if all else failed, he still had one scientific profession open to him. Then the heavy door swung open, and the old boxer led them in.
A gravel path wound up through the garden, which was full of holes and mounds of earth. It looked, Watson thought, as if a giant had dug it over, searching for something he had lost.

A stout, frightened woman, Mrs Bernstone the housekeeper, hurried out to meet them at the door. She cried that Mr Bartholomew had locked himself in his room, and that she had heard nothing from him for hours.
Mrs Bernstone took Miss Morstan into her own warm room, saying that no young lady should see what might be upstairs. Thaddeus, Holmes and Watson climbed the dark stairs together.
They knocked at the door and called, but there was no reply. Thaddeus bent to look through the keyhole, then sprang back with a cry and clutched Holmes's arm, white as chalk.
Holmes looked through the keyhole himself and became very grave. He and Watson put their shoulders to the door, and after two or three heavy blows it burst from its hinges.
In the middle of the room Bartholomew Sholto sat in a high chair, quite dead. His head hung to one side, and his face was frozen in a terrible, unnatural smile.
The room was crowded with books, bottles and strange instruments, and the window was shut. The key was in the lock on the inside, so how had anyone come in?
Watson felt for a pulse and knew at once that Bartholomew had been dead for some hours. The body was stiff, and the awful smile did not change.
Then Watson noticed a long, dark thorn stuck in the skin above the dead man's ear. Holmes drew it out with care and said that it looked like a thorn from some kind of tree.
Watson said that the twisted face looked like the work of a powerful poison. Holmes agreed, and he added that the thorn was the most likely way of delivering it.
On the table lay a scrap of paper covered with an untidy scrawl. It said, “The sign of the four,” in a rough, untidy hand.
Thaddeus wrung his hands and wailed that the police would say that he had killed his brother. Holmes told him sternly that the police must be sent for, and that he should say nothing but the truth.
McMurdo was sent running to the nearest police station, and Watson went downstairs to tell Mary. She listened, pale but steady, and said only that she was sorry for the poor brothers.
Holmes took out his lens and went over the room inch by inch, crawling on the floor like a hound. He studied the window, the door and the floor, and he muttered to himself as he went.
At last Holmes stopped under a small square hole in the ceiling, which led up towards the roof. He said that this was the way the murderer had come, and he pulled himself up through it.
Holmes called Watson up through the hole, and they stood together in a dark, dusty space under the roof. On the floor were tiny prints of a bare foot, marked with a dark stain.
Holmes said that the prints were stained with creosote, a dark tar with a strong smell. A good dog, he added, would be able to follow it wherever the little man had gone.
Holmes found a small opening in the roof and looked out into the dark. He said that the little man could not have climbed so high alone, so a second person must have helped him.
In the soft earth below the house Holmes found a boot print and, beside it, a round hole. He said that it was the mark of a wooden leg, made by a man who had waited there.
Inspector Athelney Jones of Scotland Yard arrived with two constables, a large, loud man with great self-confidence. He told Holmes that this case was plain and that he did not need any help.

Jones decided that Thaddeus had killed his brother for the treasure, and he arrested him on the spot. He also took the housekeeper and the servants, and Holmes told him gently that he was making a mistake.
Holmes told the Inspector that the real murderers were two men, one with a wooden leg and one very small. Jones laughed, but Holmes said that he would find them very soon.
Holmes sent Watson to take Mary safely home to Mrs Forrester's, and they drove away together. They said little, because there was too much on both their minds.
At Mrs Forrester's door Mary thanked him warmly and gave him her hand. Walking away, Watson realised that if the treasure were hers she would be rich, and that he had no right to love a rich woman.

When Watson reached Baker Street, Holmes had found a book about the Andaman Islands, in the Bay of Bengal. He read aloud that its small people were fierce, and that they used blowpipes and poisoned darts.
In the grey light before sunrise Holmes and Watson walked to Pinchin Lane, a narrow street near the river. They stopped at a shabby house with a faded sign, and Holmes knocked hard on the door.
A window opened above them, and a cross voice demanded to know who was making that noise. Holmes said that he needed the dog Toby, and that he would pay well.
Mr Sherman, a thin old man, let them in, and they followed him through a room full of strange noises. Cages hung on every wall, and stuffed birds stared down from the shelves with glass eyes.
Sherman led out Toby, an ugly, brown and white dog with long, floppy ears and a clumsy, waddling walk. Holmes said that he was worth ten of any beautiful hound, because of his wonderful nose.
Holmes gave Sherman half a sovereign and promised to bring the dog back safe and sound. Sherman handed over the lead and warned them that Toby was shy of strangers but loyal to anyone who was kind.
They took a cab back to Upper Norwood, with Toby sitting between them on the seat, looking out of the window. The sun was just rising, and the fog was beginning to thin.
At Pondicherry Lodge a policeman stood on guard, and he let them pass when Holmes explained. Holmes showed Toby the tarry footprints by the wall, and the dog gave a short bark and set off.

They followed Toby for mile after mile, past houses and gardens, while the sun rose and the first workmen went to their jobs. People stopped to stare at the two gentlemen who were hurrying after a dog.

Months later Small heard that Sholto had left the army and was living in England as a rich man. He understood at once that he had been cheated, and he felt a bitter rage.

Small and Tonga crept into the garden with a long rope, and Small threw one end up to the roof. Tonga, who could climb as easily as a cat, went up it hand over hand and vanished through an opening in the roof.
