When the colour had come back to her cheeks, she said very quietly that she had feared it for a long time.

Thaddeus settled himself by the hookah, drew a few puffs from it to calm his nerves and began his story. His father, Major John Sholto, had served in India alongside Captain Morstan, and he had come home to England with enough money to buy a fine house at Upper Norwood. He had lived there, however, in an unhappy state of fear that nobody could explain.

The old Major lived in terror of one-legged men, and for years he never ventured out of doors without a strong guard of hired boxers. On one occasion, seeing a harmless tradesman with a wooden leg at his gate, he fired a revolver at him in blind panic, and he had to pay a large sum to keep the matter quiet. Not even his own sons knew what lay behind this strange and bitter fear, and he would never speak of it to anyone.

In December 1878, said Thaddeus, Captain Morstan had come to Pondicherry Lodge to claim his rightful share of a great treasure that the Major had brought from India. The friends had quarrelled bitterly over it, and in the midst of the quarrel Captain Morstan had clutched at his chest and fallen dead, striking his head upon the corner of the iron chest. The Major, afraid that nobody would believe in a natural death, had hidden the body with the help of an old servant.

Thaddeus explained that the Major had hidden the body and told nobody, because he feared that the world would call him a murderer and take the treasure away. From that night he was never at peace, for he saw danger in every shadow and in every stranger at the gate. The years passed, and his health, which had never been strong, began to fail.

In the spring of 1882 the old Major took to his bed, and the doctors told his sons that he would not live much longer. He sent for his twin sons, Thaddeus and Bartholomew, and asked them to sit one on each side of him in the lamplit room. His voice was weak and broken, but there was a strange urgency in it that made both of his sons hold their breath.

In a whisper the old man told them of the great treasure that he had brought from India, and of the death of Captain Morstan, and he admitted that he had done a wrong to Morstan's daughter. He wished, he said, to put it right before he died, and he began to tell them where the jewels were hidden. His sons leaned closer over the bed, hardly daring to breathe, in order to catch every word that fell from his lips.

Suddenly the dying man sat up, stared in horror at the window and cried that the man must be kept out, for the love of God. His sons turned and saw a bearded face with wild, glittering eyes pressed against the glass, and then, in an instant, it was gone. When they ran to the window they found nothing but the empty garden and the night.

The old man fell back on his pillows and died before he could finish his sentence, and the secret of the hiding place went with him. In the morning his sons found that the room had been searched and the window left open, and on the dead man's chest lay a scrap of paper. On it, in an untidy hand, were the words “the sign of the four.”

For six long years the twin brothers searched the house from cellar to roof, and Bartholomew, who had grown more and more obsessed, had the whole garden dug up in his hunt for the hidden jewels. They found nothing at all, and the long strain of failure sharpened the old differences between the brothers into bitter quarrels. Thaddeus, who was gentler and more nervous, finally took rooms of his own and left his brother to the search.

Thaddeus, who could not forget that Mary Morstan had been wronged, feared that she might be living in want. Every year, therefore, he sent her one of the few large pearls that his father had left, though he dared not do more while his brother held the keys of the house. He had hoped that the pearls would keep her from hardship until the treasure was found.

Only a short time ago, Bartholomew had measured the whole house with a rule and found that its inside was shorter than its outside, and he guessed that a space had been hidden under the roof. He broke through a ceiling in the upper part of the house, and there, in the dust, lay the iron chest that had been hidden for years. When he lifted the lid, he found that the whole of the Agra treasure lay there untouched, shining in the lamplight like a handful of stars.

The brothers stood together gazing upon a heap of diamonds, rubies and emeralds, such as few men ever see in the course of a long life. Thaddeus said at once that Mary Morstan must have her fair share, though he feared that his twin, who had grown hard and greedy, would never agree without gentle persuasion. It was for this reason, he explained, that he had arranged the meeting at the Lyceum and brought her in secret.

Thaddeus insisted that they must all go to his brother's house together at once, for he was afraid that Bartholomew would change his mind or do something rash. A carriage was already waiting at the door, and the little man, wrapped in a heavy coat, urged them into it with nervous haste. They rolled away through the fog towards Upper Norwood, and Mary sat quietly between the two men.

The carriage went on for many miles through the foggy darkness, and the little man talked nervously all the way. He spoke of his pictures, his heart, his hatred of the police and his wish to do justice to Miss Morstan, until Holmes, who wanted quiet to think, said gently that the story would keep until they arrived. Thaddeus fell silent at once, though his small hands never stopped moving restlessly upon his knee, and his eyes darted from one window of the carriage to the other.

At last the carriage halted beside a high stone wall, topped with broken glass, in which a single small door was set, strengthened with iron. Thaddeus rapped on it with a peculiar knock, and from the dark on the other side a deep and gruff voice demanded to know who was there. The little man replied that it was he, and begged to be let in.

The door opened a hand's breadth, and a huge, broad-shouldered man with a lantern peered out at them, his battered face grim and suspicious. It was McMurdo, a retired boxer, and he told Thaddeus bluntly that his master had given strict orders that nobody was to be admitted. He knew Mr Thaddeus well enough, he said, but he did not know his friends.

Holmes stepped forward into the lantern light and reminded the boxer that they had fought three rounds together some years before, on the night of the man's benefit. McMurdo stared, burst out laughing and cried that if Mr Holmes had only stood up and landed that cross-hit of his under the jaw, he would have known him without any question. He lamented, with a wide grin, that so fine a talent had been wasted on a detective.

Holmes whispered to Watson, with a quiet chuckle, that if all else failed him he still had one of the scientific professions open to him. Then the heavy door swung wide, and the old boxer, still grinning, stepped aside and held up his lantern to light their way. Beyond it lay a great dark garden, and the air smelt of damp earth.

A gravel path wound towards the house between great heaps of raw earth, and on either side the ground was pitted with holes, as if a whole army of gardeners had been digging for lost treasure. Watson thought it a dreary, desolate sight, more like a quarry than a garden. Against the sky the dark mass of the house rose gloomy and silent, with scarcely a light in any window.

The housekeeper, Mrs Bernstone, a stout and anxious woman in a neat cap, came hurrying out to meet them and cried that she was thankful they had come. Mr Bartholomew had locked himself in his room, she said, and in all the hours since then she had heard no sound at all, and no answer had come to her calling. She had a dreadful fear, she added, that something terrible had happened to him, for he was not a man who ever kept silent for long.

Mrs Bernstone took Miss Morstan kindly by the arm and led her into her own warm room, saying that no young lady ought to see whatever might be upstairs. The three men climbed the dark, creaking staircase, with Thaddeus, whose teeth were chattering, following a step behind the others. A narrow passage led to a door at the far end, and there was no light under it.

They knocked and shouted at the door, but nothing answered them except a deep, unnatural quiet that seemed to press upon the whole house. Thaddeus bent down to the keyhole, looked for a moment and then recoiled with a high, thin cry, clutching at Holmes's arm with a hand as cold as ice. It was his brother's face, he gasped, with a ghastly and horrible grin upon it.

Holmes took Thaddeus's place at the keyhole, looked for a long moment and straightened up with a face that had grown very grave. He and Watson then threw themselves together against the door, once, twice and a third time, until the lock gave way with a crash. The door burst inwards, and the candle-light from the passage spilled into the silent room.

In the middle of the room, under the light of a lamp, Bartholomew Sholto sat in a high chair with his head thrown back and to one side. His face was frozen into a dreadful, unnatural smile, and his hands were clenched in his lap. Watson, who had seen death in many forms, felt his skin creep at the sight.

The room was part study and part workshop, with tables crowded with books, glass bottles and curious instruments, and a lamp burning steadily on the desk. The window was fastened on the inside, and the key stood in the lock of the broken door, exactly where its owner had left it. Whoever had killed Bartholomew Sholto, it seemed, had either passed through solid walls or had known some secret way that no one else suspected.

Watson bent over the dead man, felt for a pulse that was no longer there and knew at once that Bartholomew had been dead for several hours. The limbs were stiff and the face was fixed, and there was something in the strange contortion of the muscles that suggested a violent and sudden agony. It was unlike anything that the doctor had seen, even in the hospitals and on the battlefields of Afghanistan, and it filled him with dread.

Then Watson noticed, half hidden in the hair above the dead man's ear, a long dark thorn stuck deep into the skin. Holmes drew it out with the greatest care, turned it in the light and observed that it was not the kind of thing that one expects to find in an English house. He said nothing more for a while, but his eyes were bright with the look of a hound that has caught the scent of its prey.

Watson observed that the twisted limbs and the dreadful smile were exactly what a strong poison of a certain kind might produce. Holmes, holding the thorn to the lamp, agreed that it must have carried the poison into the body, for it was a clever and cruel weapon that would leave only a tiny scratch. Neither man could yet explain how it had been used in a room that was shut.

On the table beside the dead man lay a scrap of paper, and on it, scrawled in a rough and untidy hand, were the same four words that Mary's old plan had borne. Holmes read them aloud, as one reads a verdict, and then asked who in the world could have written them. Thaddeus, who stared at the paper in horror, cried that the same words had been left on his father's dead body six years before.

Thaddeus wrung his hands and wailed that the police would surely say that he had killed his brother, since he was the one who stood to gain by the death. Holmes told him sharply that nothing could be worse than hiding the matter, and that a message must be sent at once to the nearest police station. He added that Thaddeus had only to tell the truth, and that he would be in no danger if he did.

The old boxer was sent running to the nearest police station with a note, and Watson went downstairs to break the news to Mary. She listened in silence, very pale but perfectly steady, and said only that she was sorry for the poor brothers who had come to such an end. In that moment Watson felt more strongly than ever how brave and gentle she was.

Holmes took out his lens and set about the room as methodically as a surgeon, crawling over the floor, peering into the corners and examining the window, the walls and the broken door inch by inch. Now and then he gave a low murmur of satisfaction or sprang up to study some small mark in the light. He worked in complete silence, with the absorbed look of a man who sees what others cannot, and Watson knew better than to disturb him.

At last Holmes stopped beneath a small square opening in the ceiling, a trap that led up into the dark space beneath the roof, and stared at it with a look of triumph. The murderer, he declared, must have come and gone by that road, since there was no other. He leaped, caught the edge with both hands and drew himself lightly up through the hole and out of sight.

Holmes called to Watson to join him, and the doctor pulled himself up through the hole into a low, dusty garret under the roof. In the dust, by the light of the lantern, there were plainly visible the prints of small bare feet, so small that they might have belonged to a child, and dark with some sticky stain. Holmes bent over them with delight, as a hunter might over the first sign of his quarry.

Holmes sniffed at the marks and announced that they were stained with creosote, that dark and pungent tar which is used to preserve wood and fences. A good dog, he observed with satisfaction, would be able to follow so strong a scent through half of London if he were given the chance. He had already decided, he said, exactly where such a dog might be found, and he meant to go and fetch it before the sun was up.

Holmes found a narrow opening in the slope of the roof and thrust his head out into the foggy night, where the lights of London glimmered faintly far away. A man so small and so light might have climbed in this way, he said, but never without help from below, which meant that there had been at least two people in the plot. He drew his head in again, brushed the dust from his sleeves and said that they should go down at once to the garden, before the fog and the dew could spoil any marks.

In the soft earth at the foot of the wall, Holmes found the clear print of a boot and, beside it, a round deep hole such as a wooden peg leaves behind. He measured the distance between the prints with his tape and declared that the man had a long stride and a strong build. This, he said, was the mark of one who had waited below while his small companion made the climb.

Inspector Athelney Jones of Scotland Yard arrived with two constables, a stout, red-faced man of enormous self-importance, who recognised Holmes at once and greeted him with a patronising smile. This was a plain case, he announced, and one that did not need the help of theorists, since he had already seen what had happened. Holmes, who had worked with him before, listened with great patience and a faint smile.

Jones declared that Thaddeus Sholto had murdered his brother to keep the whole treasure for himself, and he arrested the little man on the spot, together with the housekeeper and the other members of the household. Thaddeus protested in a thin, trembling voice that he was innocent, and that the whole affair had been done by some other hand. Holmes warned the Inspector quietly that he was making a very serious mistake, and that the real criminals were at that moment far away from the house.

Holmes explained, in a few clear sentences, that the murderers were two men, one of whom had a wooden leg and the other a small, bare, tar-stained foot, and that they had entered by the roof. Jones laughed loudly and said that it was a pretty story, but that he preferred plain facts. Holmes only smiled, and said that he would have the guilty men by the end of the week, and that Jones would be welcome to help.

Holmes asked Watson to take Miss Morstan safely back to Mrs Forrester's house, and the two of them drove away together in a cab through the thinning fog. They said little, for the horror of the evening lay heavily upon both of them, and each was lost in thought. The only sound was the steady beat of the horse's hooves on the road.

At Mrs Forrester's door Mary thanked him warmly and gave him her hand, and he felt it tremble in his. As he walked away, Watson realised that if the treasure were found, she would become a rich woman, and that a half-pay doctor with a wounded leg had no right to offer her his love. He was ashamed to find that, deep down, he hoped that the treasure would never be found.

When Watson reached Baker Street in the early hours, Holmes had already found a heavy book on the Andaman Islands and was reading aloud from it with growing excitement. Their people, it said, were among the smallest in the world, a fierce and suspicious race, yet capable of devoted friendships and skilled with poisoned darts shot from a blowpipe. Holmes laid the dark thorn upon the page and said that it was a clue worth following, and that they must fetch a dog at first light.

Before the sun was up, Holmes and Watson made their way through the empty, echoing streets to Pinchin Lane, a narrow and shabby little road not far from the river. They stopped at the door of a small, untidy house, where a faded board announced that Mr Sherman stuffed birds and beasts. Holmes beat upon the door with his fist until the sound rolled up and down the lane.

A window above them flew open, and a hoarse and angry voice demanded to know who dared to wake a respectable man at such an hour. Holmes called up that he was an old friend who needed the dog Toby for a few hours, and that he was ready to pay handsomely. There was a long, grumbling silence, and then came the sound of slow footsteps on the stairs.

Mr Sherman, a stooping old fellow in a dressing-gown, let them in at last, and they followed his lamp through a room that seemed more like a zoo than a house. Cages hung from every hook, small creatures rustled and squeaked in the dark, and rows of stuffed birds stared down from the shelves with bright glass eyes. The air was warm and full of the smell of straw, feathers and animals.

Mr Sherman fetched Toby from a back room, a long-haired, lop-eared dog, half spaniel and half lurcher, brown and white in colour, and quite remarkably ugly. He walked with a clumsy, waddling gait and looked up at the visitors with a pair of sleepy, mournful eyes. Holmes, however, declared that he was worth a dozen handsome hounds, for no dog in London could follow a scent so well.

Holmes counted half a sovereign into the old man's palm and promised faithfully that Toby would be brought back safe and sound before the day was over. Sherman, who had suddenly become very polite, handed over the lead and warned them that the dog was shy of strangers but would follow anyone who spoke to him kindly. He added, with evident pride, that Toby was the finest tracker he had ever known.

They drove back towards Upper Norwood in a hired cab, with Toby squatting happily on the seat between them and gazing out of the window at the passing houses as if he were a gentleman of leisure. The sun was just beginning to rise, and the fog that had hung over the city all night was thinning into pale ribbons. Watson, who had not slept at all and had seen two terrible sights that night, found that he was strangely cheerful in the morning air.

At Pondicherry Lodge a lone constable stood on guard at the gate, and he let them pass as soon as Holmes explained who they were. Holmes led the dog to the foot of the wall, where the tarry prints were still plain, and held his nose close to them. Toby gave a short, eager whine, wagged his tail, and set off through the garden at a quick, waddling trot.

They followed Toby for mile after mile, along quiet villa roads and busy main streets, while the sun climbed over the roofs and the first workmen went trudging to their labour. Carts rattled past, shop shutters came down with a clatter, and people stopped to stare at the two gentlemen who were hurrying after a dog. Holmes paid no attention to them whatever, and kept his eyes fixed upon the little brown shape ahead.

After an hour of this, Watson began to wonder how any dog could keep a single thread of scent through all the odours of a great city. Holmes, who strode along with his hands behind him and his eyes bright, told him that creosote was a smell like no other, and that a dog with such a nose would not lose it. Watson said nothing more, but his wounded leg was beginning to ache badly, and he could not help wishing that the dog would stop.

At last the little dog turned in at the open gate of a great timber yard, where tall stacks of planks stood in long rows like the streets of a miniature town. He ran between them with his nose to the ground and his tail quivering with excitement, while the two men hurried after, wondering where the trail would end. Suddenly he stopped, gave a sharp bark and darted towards a far corner of the yard, where something large and round stood in the shadow.

Toby dashed to a large wooden barrel in the corner of the yard, planted himself beside it and looked up at them with the air of a dog who has done his duty. The barrel, when Watson sniffed at it, was filled with creosote, and the smell hung heavy in the air all round it. Holmes stared at the barrel for a long moment, and then, to Watson's great surprise, he leaned back and burst out laughing.

A moment later Holmes understood what had happened, and he laughed at his own mistake, for the barrel explained everything. The little man had trodden in creosote here, before he ever climbed to the roof of Pondicherry Lodge, and Toby, with his faithful nose, had followed the tracks back to the very place where they began. They had gone, in short, the wrong way, and the end of the trail lay somewhere behind them.

Holmes called Toby away from the barrel, and the two men walked him slowly round the edge of the yard, so that he might find the scent where it left the place. For several minutes the little dog ran this way and that, sniffing and whining, while Watson began to fear that the trail was lost for good. Then, all at once, his tail went up, and he darted out of the gate and along the road.

The trail now led down a narrow lane between tall, gloomy warehouses, and Watson smelled the river long before he saw it, with its odours of mud, tar and coal smoke. Soon they came out upon a wide stretch of muddy shore, where a little wooden landing stage ran out into the water and a few small boats lay tilted on their sides. Toby trotted out upon the damp planks with his nose still down, and stopped at the very end, where there was nothing left to follow.

The dog stood at the very end of the landing stage, looking down at the grey water and then up at Holmes with a puzzled air, as if to ask what was to be done next. The trail ended there, for the river carries no scent, and it was obvious that the two fugitives had left the shore by boat. Holmes stood for a long time in thought, gazing at the tide as it ran past the piles.

Near the landing stage stood a little wooden house with a pair of oars leaning against its wall, and Holmes went up to it and knocked to ask about the boats that used the place. It was opened by a woman with an anxious face and reddened eyes, who wiped her hands on her apron as she listened. She said that her name was Mrs Smith, and that the boats of the place belonged to her husband.

Mrs Smith told them that her husband, Mordecai Smith, owned a steam launch called the Aurora, a trim black boat with a tall funnel, which was the swiftest craft on that part of the river. He took parties up and down the water for hire, she said, and he was known to be a careful man. Holmes, who was listening with the closest attention, asked her where the Aurora was now.

Mrs Smith said that her husband had taken the Aurora out with his son Jim, and that neither of them had returned. He had told her only that he had a job to do and would be back soon, and she had no notion of where he had gone, or with whom. Her voice shook, and it was plain that she had been worrying for a long time.

Holmes thanked her with a courteous bow and led Watson away from the house, speaking in a low voice as they went. The Aurora, he said, was now the most important vessel in London, because it had almost certainly carried the two criminals and their prize away. If they could find the launch, he added, they would find the men, and they must not lose a moment.

They returned Toby to Mr Sherman, who greeted the weary dog with delight, and then Holmes and Watson took a cab back to Baker Street, where the morning sun was shining brightly on the windows. Watson, who had not closed his eyes all night and had walked more miles than he cared to count, was asleep before the cab had gone half-way. Holmes alone remained wide awake, with his thin face set in thought and his keen eyes fixed on the grey line of the river far behind them.

Watson slept for several hours, and when he awoke he found that the sun had moved across the room and that Holmes, who had not rested at all, was pacing up and down with his hands clasped behind him. They could not search the whole length of the river between them, he said, and the police were too slow and too easily seen. He had therefore decided, he said, to send for his own private army, which was small, ragged and quite remarkably efficient.

A moment later there was a clatter of boots on the stairs, and about a dozen of the dirtiest and most ragged street boys that Watson had ever seen crowded into the room. They were the Baker Street Irregulars, the eyes and ears of the poorer streets of London, and their leader, a sharp-eyed little fellow called Wiggins, stepped forward and saluted. Holmes greeted him gravely and courteously, exactly as if he were a general who had come to report upon a famous campaign.

Holmes told the boys that they must search every wharf, dock and boatyard along the river, as far as they could go, for a steam launch called the Aurora, a small black boat with a tall funnel. They were not to go aboard, he said, but only to find where she lay and to report to him at once. The boys listened in complete silence, their sharp little faces full of pride and attention, and not one of them asked a single question.

Holmes promised each of the boys a shilling for his day's work and a whole guinea to the one who should find the Aurora, and the little group of thin, hungry faces lit up like lamps. They gave a ragged cheer, wheeled round with surprising discipline and clattered away down the stairs, and a moment later they were scattered across London. Watson marvelled that so much energy could be hidden in so small a space.

Holmes disappeared into his bedroom and came out, to Watson's amazement, as a bent and weather-beaten old seaman, with a grey beard, a rough blue coat and a pipe that was already smelling most abominably. He said that he meant to look into the riverside inns and boatyards himself, since there were things that boys could not ask. Then he shuffled down the stairs and out into the street, and the door banged behind him.

Watson stayed in the sitting room for the rest of the day, trying to read the newspapers and to ignore the silence, but his ears were always listening for a step upon the stairs. The hours dragged past with a tedious slowness, and the light faded in the windows until the lamps in the street were lit. Still nobody came, and he began to wonder whether his friend had met with some misfortune.

Late in the evening there came a shuffling step upon the stair, and a bent and weather-beaten old seaman stood in the doorway, so unlike Holmes that Watson rose and asked him sharply what he wanted. Then the figure straightened, threw back its head and began to laugh, and in that laugh Watson recognised his friend. It was, Watson had to admit, the most perfect disguise that he had ever seen.

Holmes sat down, tore the beard from his chin and ate a plain supper with the appetite of a hungry wolf. He explained between mouthfuls that he had asked in a dozen yards and public houses without hearing a word of the Aurora, but that the boys would find her, since they could go where a gentleman could not. In the meantime there was nothing to do but wait, and he proposed that they should both get some sleep.

By the next morning the newspapers were full of the Norwood mystery, which they described in the most lurid terms, and every column praised Inspector Jones for his speed in arresting the brother of the dead man. Holmes read the articles aloud at the breakfast table, with a dry and sardonic smile, and remarked that the Inspector would soon learn how little his clever arrests were worth. Then he put the paper down, folded his long arms and looked towards the window, as though the answer to all his troubles might be seen upon the river.

In the afternoon Wiggins returned with his troop, tired and muddy and as hungry as wolves, and reported that nobody had seen so much as a trace of the Aurora in any boatyard they had searched. Holmes thanked them gravely, paid them for the day and sent them out again to search farther down the river, towards the sea. It was plain to Watson that his friend was fighting a growing fear that the launch had already left the Thames.

Two days went by without a single word of the Aurora, and Holmes grew more irritable and more restless with every hour that passed. He smoked pipe after pipe until the room was blue with smoke, paced the carpet until it seemed likely to wear through, and answered Watson's questions with short, sharp snaps. It was the idle mind that tormented him, and Watson, who knew it well, kept a respectful silence.

Watson found it necessary to call upon Miss Morstan, for the sake of her anxiety, as he told himself, and he told her everything that had happened since the dreadful night at Pondicherry Lodge. She listened with close attention, her large blue eyes on his face, and she asked a good many sensible questions about the dog, the boat and the little man on the roof. Watson found, to his own surprise, that he was in no hurry at all to go, and that the afternoon had slipped away like water.

Mary poured out the tea herself, and as they sat together she said, with her simple honesty, that she did not think a fortune would make her any happier than she was now. Watson's heart leaped at the words, for he had feared that she would dream of the jewels, and he felt a warmth that had nothing to do with the fire. Yet he could not forget that the treasure, if it were found, would place her far above him.

Mrs Forrester, who had been watching the two young people with a kindly twinkle in her eye, said as he rose to leave that he must come again whenever he had any news. Watson thanked her rather more warmly than the occasion required, and walked home in the rain without noticing the wet. He felt that for the first time in months his life had a pleasant direction.

On the evening of the third day a tired and muddy little boy came pounding up the stairs with news that made Holmes spring from his chair. He had seen a black steam launch with a tall funnel in a small boatyard on the south side of the river, he gasped, and the men there were busy loading coal as though they meant to put to sea. Holmes pressed a golden guinea into his grubby hand and sent him to fetch Wiggins.

Holmes wrote a hasty note to Inspector Jones, and within the hour that officer was sitting at the table in Baker Street, smoking a cigar and wearing a frown that was half doubt and half curiosity. Holmes explained to him, in a few sharp sentences, that the murderers were in a launch called the Aurora, and that a fast police boat was needed on the river that very evening. Jones, who was a practical man at heart, said that it could be arranged.

Jones admitted, a little sourly, that he had been obliged to release Thaddeus Sholto and the whole household, because there was no proof against them. The little man had been miles away at the time of the murder, he said, and Mr Holmes had been right about the wooden leg. It cost him an effort to say it, but he said it handsomely, and he offered to place the river police at Holmes's disposal.

Watson took his old army revolver from the drawer where it had lain since his return from Afghanistan, and loaded it with careful fingers, while Holmes put on a thick coat and slipped a pistol into the pocket. Jones, meanwhile, finished his cigar and said that the launch would be waiting at Westminster Stairs. It was a cold, clear evening, and the first lamps were beginning to shine in the street.

At Westminster Stairs a smart police launch lay waiting at the foot of the stone steps, her engine murmuring and a thin thread of steam hissing from her funnel. Jones introduced the steersman and two men to tend the fire, and the three of them climbed aboard, with Holmes taking his place in the bow. The water slapped softly against her sides, and above them the great clock of Westminster began to strike.

The launch slid out into the stream and glided down the dark river under the great bridges, past silent wharves, tall warehouses and long lines of moored barges, while the last daylight faded in the sky. Jones said little, though he watched the water ahead with the unblinking attention of a cat at a mouse-hole. Holmes, who stood in the bow, was as still as a carved figure, and Watson knew that he was hunting.

Near the boatyard on the south bank the police launch slipped quietly into the deep shadow of a line of moored barges, where she lay as still as a log. Jones ordered every light to be put out, and the engine was allowed to murmur so softly that it could scarcely be heard above the lapping of the water. The yard stood a hundred yards ahead, a dark huddle of sheds and posts against the sky.

The three men waited in silence while the cold crept up from the water and into their very bones, and the minutes seemed to stretch into hours. The only sounds were the creak of the barges, the soft lap of the tide and the faint hiss of steam from the funnel, and now and then a distant bell struck the quarter. Watson, with his pistol in his pocket, felt a nervous excitement that he had not known since Afghanistan.

Holmes leaned towards Watson and whispered that the little man whose footprints they had seen would almost certainly be armed with a blowpipe and poisoned darts. If he were given time to use them, he said, any one of them might die in a moment, and so they must shoot first and ask questions afterwards. Watson nodded, with a dry mouth, and felt for the cold butt of his revolver.

Suddenly, out of the mouth of the boatyard, a long black launch glided into the stream, with a shower of sparks flying from her tall funnel and a white wake spreading behind her. A tall figure stood at the wheel, and a small dark shape crouched in the bow, and Holmes said very softly that this was the Aurora at last. Not a light showed on board, and she seemed to be creeping out like a thief.

Jones leaped to his feet and shouted across the water, in the loudest voice that he could command, that the launch must stop in the name of the law. The answer was a sudden surge of speed, for the Aurora sprang forward like a frightened horse, with the black water curling up on either side of her bow. The police launch's lamps flared on, her engine began to roar, and the men below began to heap more coal upon the furnace.

Jones bawled to the two men at the furnace that they must give her every ounce of steam that she could bear, and they fell to shovelling coal until the little fire-box roared like a wild beast. The police launch shook from stem to stern and sprang forward, and the great chase down the Thames began. On either bank the lights of London began to stream past like threads of gold.

The Aurora proved to be a splendid boat, built for speed and perfectly handled, and for a long while she kept her distance in spite of all that the police launch could do. Mile after mile they hurtled down the river, past anchored ships, dark wharves and the glimmering lights of the docks, while the wind whipped spray into their faces. Holmes, his eyes shining, said that it was the finest sport that he had ever known.

In the red glare from the Aurora's furnace, Watson could now see her crew plainly, and the sight made him catch his breath. A tall man stood at the wheel, holding the launch to her course with the stiffness of a statue, and in the bow a small black figure crouched like an animal. The little figure seemed to be fumbling with something at its lips, and Watson felt the hair rise on the back of his neck.

Slowly, very slowly, the heavier police launch began to gain upon the Aurora, as the furnace roared and the engine thudded like the beating of a great heart. The gap shrank from a hundred yards to fifty, and then to less, until the two crews could see each other's faces in the flickering light of the fires. On both boats every man held his breath, and even the engines seemed to throb more softly while the last yards were slowly eaten up.

When the boats were no more than a few lengths apart, the small crouching figure in the bow suddenly rose, lifted a long pipe to his lips and turned his head towards them. Holmes and Watson, who had been waiting for precisely this moment, raised their pistols together. For a fraction of a second the whole world seemed to stand still, and there was no sound anywhere except the roar of the two engines.

Holmes and Watson fired together, and the two sharp reports rolled across the water like a single clap of thunder. The little man gave a strange, strangled cry, threw up both his arms and toppled sideways into the dark river, where he vanished without leaving so much as a ripple. A moment later something whistled past Holmes's head and stuck quivering in the woodwork behind him.

The black water closed over the little man, and nobody on either boat ever saw him again, and for one moment the whole river seemed to hold its breath. Then the tall man at the Aurora's wheel gave a hoarse and furious cry, shook his fist at the police launch and swung his boat sharply towards the bank. It was a desperate move, made in a blind rage, and there was nothing in it at all of cunning or of hope.

The Aurora swerved across the stream, ploughed into a bank of soft mud with a heavy shock and stuck fast, with her screw still churning furiously in the shallows and her funnel shaking. The police launch, which had no time to stop, swept in beside her and ran aground only a few yards away, throwing everyone off their feet. Jones scrambled up, shouting orders, and his men leaped over the side into the shallow water.

The tall man leaped from the stern of the Aurora on to the bank, but his wooden leg sank deep into the soft mud and held him fast, so that he could not move an inch. He tugged and cursed and struggled like a fly in treacle, until Jones's men reached him, threw a rope round his shoulders and dragged him out on to firm ground. He was a ragged, weather-beaten fellow with a hard face, and he took his defeat with a sullen calm.

Holmes looked at the prisoner for a long moment and said, quietly, that he believed he was addressing Jonathan Small, whose name had stood first on an old plan in a lady's possession. The man nodded without surprise, and asked in a low voice whether his little friend had been hit. When Holmes told him that the little man had fallen into the river, a shadow of real grief crossed his hard face.

Jones and his men searched the stranded Aurora from end to end with their lanterns, turning over coils of rope, sacks of coal and oily rags. In the cramped little cabin they found a heavy iron box with a stout padlock, hidden under a blanket, and Jones's eyes shone with the joy of a man who has made a great discovery. He lifted one end with a grunt, and remarked, with a puzzled frown, that it was surprisingly light for a chest of treasure.

Jones wished to carry the box straight to the police station, as the regulations required, but Holmes argued that Miss Morstan had the first claim to it. She ought to be the first to see what it contained, he said, and Watson should take it to her that very night, while Small told his story afterwards at Baker Street. Jones grumbled for some time, but he was at heart a fair-minded man, and in the end he agreed to the plan.

At last, with a great deal of heaving and shouting, the two boats were pulled off the mud, and the little party began the long journey back up the river. The prisoner sat quietly in the stern between two policemen, while the tide turned, the wind dropped and a few pale stars appeared between the clouds. Nobody on board felt much inclined to talk, for the excitement had drained away and left only a heavy weariness behind it.

Holmes sat in the bow with his pipe glowing in the darkness and told Watson, in a low and contented voice, that the case was almost finished. There remained only the question of the treasure itself, he said, and the story of how and why the whole terrible business had begun. He added that he would ask Small to tell it that same night, over a glass and a cigar.

Watson sat beside the iron box all the way, with his hand resting upon its cold lid, and thought of Mary Morstan and what its contents might mean for her. If the box were full, she would be a wealthy woman, and the gulf between a rich heiress and a poor doctor would be wider than ever. It was a selfish thought, and he tried in vain to be rid of it.

They landed at Westminster, where Jones took charge of the prisoner, and Watson took a cab with the iron box on the seat beside him, for Holmes had asked him to carry it to Mary at once. It was very late, and the streets were empty and wet, but he knew that she would be waiting up to hear the news. The cab seemed to crawl, and his heart was beating faster than the horse's hooves.

Lights still burned in Mrs Forrester's house, and Mary herself came to the door, pale but eager, with a soft grey shawl round her shoulders. She asked at once whether it was over, and whether the men who had killed Bartholomew Sholto had been caught, and Watson told her that they had, at least in part. He carried the iron box into the drawing room and set it down upon the table, and she looked at it as one looks at a sleeping animal.

The box was fastened with a stout lock, and there was no key to be found, but Mary said, with quiet determination, that she wished to see what was inside it, since it had cost her father his life. Watson fetched a heavy poker from the hearth, set its point against the hasp and leaned all his weight upon it. The lock gave way at last with a sharp crack, and the lid sprang back, and both of them leaned forward to look.

They bent over it together, with their heads almost touching, and saw in the lamplight that the box was completely empty. There was not a single jewel inside it, nor a coin, nor even a scrap of paper to say what had once been there, and the thick iron sides rang hollow under Watson's knuckles. Somebody, it was plain, had emptied it long before the police had found it.

Watson heard himself say, “Thank God,” before he could stop the words, and he knew in an instant that he had spoken them aloud. Mary turned to him with wide eyes, and asked in a gentle and puzzled voice why he should thank heaven that her fortune was gone. His face burned, and for a moment he could not find any answer at all.

Watson told her, in a low and trembling voice, that he loved her as truly as ever man loved woman, and that the treasure had sealed his lips. While she might be rich he had felt that he could not speak, for a poor doctor must not seem to be hunting a fortune, but now that the jewels were gone he was free. It was the most difficult speech that he had ever made, and the least fluent.

Mary's eyes shone, and she put her hand into his and said that she loved him too, and that she had been hoping since the first night that he would speak. She added, with a trembling little laugh, that she also thanked heaven that the jewels were gone, for they would only have stood between them. Watson felt that the whole world had changed in a moment, and that he was no longer the lonely man he had been that morning.

They sat together for a long while in a happy and contented silence, hardly needing words, and neither of them so much as glanced at the empty box. Watson thought that although the box had once been meant to hold a fortune, he himself had that evening found a far richer one. The little clock on the mantelpiece struck the hour, and for once he did not care how late it was.

At last Watson remembered that Holmes was waiting for him at Baker Street, with Inspector Jones and the prisoner, and he tore himself away from the warm drawing room. Mary came with him to the door and gave him her hand once more, and he walked out into the night as happy as a boy at the start of a holiday. It seemed to him that the lamps in the street had never shone so brightly.

At Baker Street Watson found Holmes, Jones and the prisoner gathered round the fire, with Small sitting comfortably in the best armchair, a glass at his elbow and a cigar between his lips. He looked more like a guest than a captive, and he announced that he would tell the whole truth, for he had little to lose and nothing to hide. The room fell silent, and Holmes gave a small nod of encouragement, while Jones took out his notebook and a pencil.

Small settled himself in his chair, lit a fresh cigar and said that the best way was to tell the story just as it had happened. He had been born near Pershore, in Worcestershire, he said, and as a young man he had been wild, restless and always in some kind of trouble. Holmes nodded for him to go on, and Jones turned to a clean page.

To escape his troubles he took the Queen's shilling and joined an infantry regiment that was just then going out to India, and he found, to his own surprise, that he took to soldiering very well. He was strong and quick, he said, and a very good shot, and he might have risen in the ranks in time. But his luck, as he said with a twisted smile, was never of the best kind.

One burning afternoon, after a hard day's drilling, he went swimming in the broad brown waters of the Ganges, as a good many of his comrades did, because the heat had become more than he could bear. He swam out farther than was wise, and in the golden glare he never saw the long dark shape that was gliding towards him through the water. It was the last time, he said, that he ever swam with two good legs, and he has never forgotten the cold shock of it.

A crocodile seized his leg and dragged him down, and the water around him boiled with his struggles, until a brave comrade dashed in, hauled him back to the bank and saved his life. The leg itself was gone from above the knee, however, and no surgeon could give it back. He told the story calmly, like a man who has long since stopped being surprised by it.

He lay in hospital for many weary months, and when at last he was well enough to leave it, he was told that he was no longer fit for the army and must find some other way of living. He was still young, but he was a cripple with a wooden leg, with no friends, no trade and scarcely a penny in his pocket. Those were, he said, the blackest and most hopeless days of his life, and he did not know what was to become of him.

Then, just when he was in despair, a kind-hearted planter who owned a large indigo plantation offered him work as an overseer. Small, who could ride as well with a wooden leg as most men could with two, gratefully accepted. For the first time since his accident he felt that life was worth living again, and he took real pride in making the work of the plantation run smoothly.

For some time all was quiet at the plantation, and Small thought that he had found at last a home and a purpose. But in 1857 strange rumours began to run through the countryside, whispered in the markets and along the roads, and the native soldiers seemed restless and sullen. He had no idea, he said, how near the storm had come, or how soon it would break over his own quiet little corner of the world.

Then, like a thunderbolt out of a clear sky, the great rebellion broke out, and the whole country seemed to catch fire at once. Towns burned, regiments rose against their officers, and for hundreds of miles no English man, woman or child could feel safe. Small said that it was a terrible time, and that he hoped none of them would ever see another like it.

The planter decided that the only safe place for his family was the great fort at Agra, where hundreds of English people were gathering behind its walls, and Small went with them. They travelled by night along back roads, hiding by day in the shade of the trees, and several times they heard the sound of horsemen passing by in the dark. By good luck they were never found, though more than once Small's heart nearly stopped, and he feared that his wooden leg would betray them.

The fort at Agra turned out to be an enormous place, a maze of courtyards, halls and passages that was now crowded with refugees, soldiers and sick people, while outside the walls the rebel army grew daily stronger. Small, who was a good shot, offered his services to the defenders, and because he could speak the language of the country he was soon given a post of some importance. It was there, he said, in that great crowded fortress, that the real trouble of his life was waiting for him to find it.

Small was given charge of a small gate in a far corner of the fort, a lonely and dangerous post, and three Sikh soldiers named Abdullah Khan, Mahomet Singh and Dost Akbar were placed under him. They were tall, bearded men with fierce faces and splendid manners, and they had fought bravely for the English in many a hard battle. Small came to like them very much indeed, and he trusted them more than he had ever trusted anybody in his life.

In the long, dark nights the four men sat together on the wall, watching the shadows and listening for the first sounds of an attack. They talked of home and of war and of the strange ways of their different countries, and Small, who was a ready listener, learned much of the language and the customs of the Sikhs. They in turn learned of the green fields of Worcestershire, and a man could hardly have wished for better comrades.

On one very dark night, when the rain beat down upon the wall and the wind moaned in the arches, a native merchant named Achmet came creeping up to the gate with a lantern. He looked nervous and out of breath, and under his cloak he carried a heavy bundle that clinked softly as he moved. Small, who was on watch, stopped him with a challenge, and the three Sikhs gathered silently round.

Achmet explained, in a whisper, that he was trying to save the jewels of a rich native prince from the rebels, and that he sought shelter in the fort. He opened his bundle, and diamonds, rubies and pearls flashed in the lantern light, such a sight as Small had never seen in his life. He promised a handsome share to the four guards if they would help him hide it, and the temptation was almost overwhelming.

The four guards drew aside into the shadow of the wall and whispered together, and Small confessed that the greed which came upon them then was like a fever. Why should they take a share, they asked each other, when they could take the whole of it and nobody would ever know? In that moment, he said, they were lost, though none of them knew it.

They invited Achmet into the dark passage beside the gate, as though to show him his hiding place, and there, in a moment, he was struck down before he could cry out. Small did not try to excuse the crime, for he said that it had been done by all four of them together, and the blame was shared. It was the only moment in his life, he added, that he would gladly have undone.

They hid the body in a dark corner of the fort, and with their knives and their bare hands they dug a hiding place for the treasure in the earth at the foot of a wall. They covered it with stones and rubbish until nothing could be seen, and then, with trembling hands, they went back to their posts as though nothing had happened. All night long they watched the gate in silence, and every sound from the darkness made their hearts jump.

In the following days they drew a careful plan of the fort, with a cross to mark the exact spot where the treasure lay, and each of the four signed it with his own name. They swore a solemn oath by all that they held sacred that they would be true to one another and never betray the secret, and they called their pledge the sign of the four. Small kept the paper, for he was the one who could write best, and he hid it carefully in a belt next to his skin.

Within a few months the rebellion had been crushed and the English were again masters of the country, and the fort at Agra could breathe freely once more. Small and his three comrades waited impatiently for the day when they might retrieve their prize and divide it, and plan the happy lives that it would buy them. They were never to have the chance, however, for the happy lives that they dreamed of were already slipping away from them.

But the missing merchant was soon asked after, and before long his body was found, and suspicion fell at once upon the men who had guarded the gate that night. The four of them were arrested and tried for his murder, and they were sentenced to be shut away for many years in the convict prison on the distant Andaman Islands. Small, with great care and some cunning, had managed all through this time to keep the plan hidden about his body.

The four prisoners were put on board a ship and carried across the Bay of Bengal to the Andaman Islands, a wild green place of jungle, swamp and silent beaches, where the sea beat endlessly upon the shore. Small thought that he might as well have been taken to the moon, so far was he from everything that he knew. The convict station at Port Blair was a small and gloomy settlement that lay hidden among the trees.

Life on the island was bitterly hard, with burning heat in the day, drenching rain at night and a fever that crept through the settlement and carried off many a strong man. The prisoners cleared the jungle, dug drains and built huts, and the food was poor and the guards were seldom kind. Small said that he lived through it only because he had made up his mind to live.

After a time, because he was quiet, careful and obedient, Small was given an easier post in the settlement, helping the doctor in his surgery and in his small house on the hill. He learned a little about medicine there, and he enjoyed more freedom than the other prisoners, which gave him many chances to watch and to listen. It was a position, he said, that he put to very good use, as the events of the following years were to show.

The officers who commanded the convict guard were Major Sholto and Captain Morstan, two friends who spent most of their evenings playing cards on the veranda of the doctor's house. They played for money, and they were often in debt, and Small, who was always about the house, could hear every word that they said through the open windows. He soon understood that both of them were short of money and fond of the chance of gain.

Small saw that here was his chance of freedom, and one evening, when the game was over and the officers were in a good humour, he asked leave to speak to them. He told them, in a low voice, that he knew where a great treasure lay hidden, and that he would tell them where, if they would help him in return. They listened with growing interest, and Sholto, who had been shuffling the cards, slowly put them down upon the table and leaned forward.

Sholto and Morstan agreed to go to Agra, to dig up the treasure and to share it fairly with the four prisoners. In proof of his good faith, Small handed to Captain Morstan the plan, with its four signatures and the cross that marked the hiding place, and he told them every word of the story. He had no reason at all to think that two officers and gentlemen would break their solemn promise to a poor prisoner.

Soon afterwards Sholto obtained leave of absence and went across to India, where he found the treasure in the very place that the plan showed. He did not keep his promise, however, and he left not even the smallest share for the men who had trusted him, but took everything for himself and sailed home to England. He soon retired from the army altogether, and he was never seen on the island, or heard of in those parts, again.

Months later Small learned, by one means or another, that the Major had left the army and was living in England as a rich man. He understood at once that he had been cheated out of the whole treasure, and he felt a rage so bitter that for many nights he could not sleep. From that hour, he said, he lived for one thing only, which was to face Sholto and claim his own.

Small told his three Sikh friends how they had been cheated, and they were as angry as he was, and they swore by their old oath that they would be avenged. But the island was a prison surrounded by sea and jungle, and none of them could see any way to escape from it. The years passed, and the hope of revenge grew harder and colder with each one.

Year after year Small studied the shores of the island, the habits of the guards and the moods of the sea, and waited for a chance to escape. He kept the old plan safely hidden, and he fed his hatred of the Major as a man feeds a fire in winter. Many long years of his life slipped away in this manner, and still the chance did not come.

One day, while Small was walking at the edge of the swamp beyond the settlement, he came upon a very small islander, sick, hurt and alone, who was lying among the reeds and could scarcely lift his head. Nobody else would have troubled about him, but Small, who knew what it was to be crippled and friendless, carried him back to his own hut. It was the beginning, he said, of the strangest and most faithful friendship that he had ever known in all his wandering life.

The little man's name was Tonga, and under Small's care he slowly recovered his strength, though he never lost his suspicion of strangers or his savage temper when he was crossed. He never forgot the kindness, however, and he became so devoted to Small that he followed him about like a shadow. Small taught him English words, and Tonga taught him how to handle a canoe.

Tonga had a canoe of his own, hidden among the mangroves, and he knew every inlet, current and reef of those waters as well as a farmer knows his own fields. Small, who had been waiting for so many years for a way out, began to see in his small friend the means of his escape. He said nothing about it, however, and he watched and waited a little longer, until the moment should come that was right.

Small told Tonga of his plan in a mixture of the islander's tongue and a few simple English words, and Tonga, who would have followed him anywhere, was ready at once to go with him. They chose a dark and stormy night, when the guards would be drowsy and the tide would carry them swiftly out beyond the reef. It was a desperate venture, and the odds were against them, but Small had nothing left to lose.

On the chosen night the two of them crept down to the shore, carrying a little food and water, and pushed the canoe out into the black surf. The wind howled and the rain came down in sheets, and it covered the sound of their paddles so well that nobody in the settlement saw them go. By morning the island was no more than a low green line behind them.

For several days they drifted across the open sea under a burning sun, with their food gone, their water almost finished and their lips cracked and swollen. Just when Small had begun to give up hope, a passing ship sighted the little canoe and took the two half-dead men on board. It was only then that he began to believe that he had really escaped.

In the end they reached England, where they were as poor and as friendless as any two creatures in the whole of London. They lived for years on what they could earn at fairs and shows, where crowds paid a few pence to watch Tonga dance in his island dress, and Small told them whatever tales he thought they would like to hear. It was a miserable way to live, but it kept them alive, and it kept alive also the hope that had carried them across the sea.

All this time Small had been watching for news of Major Sholto, and at last he learned that the old officer was living in a great house at Upper Norwood, in fear and in failing health. He and Tonga went there at once and looked over the high wall, and Small, who had dreamed of this day for so many years, felt his heart thump in his chest. He decided, standing there in the cold, that he would not wait another hour, and that the Major should see his face before that night was out.

That very night Small climbed to the window of the Major's room, with Tonga waiting below, and looked in at the old man, who lay in bed with his two sons beside him. The Major saw the face at the glass and knew it at once, and with one terrible cry of fear he fell back upon his pillows, dead. Small said that it was the nearest thing to justice that he had yet had, though it was not the justice that he had come for.

Later that night, when the house had fallen quiet, Small returned and climbed into the room, and he turned the whole place upside down in a fever of searching, but he found no trace of the treasure. Before he left, he wrote the four words of the old pledge on a scrap of paper and laid it on the dead man's chest, so that the Major's sons should know that the four had not forgotten. Then he and Tonga slipped away through the garden and over the wall, and vanished into the foggy darkness of the night.

For six long years Small and Tonga lived from hand to mouth in London, watching Pondicherry Lodge from a distance and never learning where the treasure was hidden. Then, at last, word reached Small through a friend that Bartholomew Sholto had found the iron chest, and that the jewels were in his keeping. They began that very night to make their plans, and they spent many hours bending over a rough sketch of the house.

Small and Tonga crept over the wall into the dark garden with a long rope that had a hook at one end, and Small threw it up until the hook caught fast on the roof. Tonga, who could climb like a cat, went up it hand over hand and vanished through the opening in the slope of the roof, while Small waited below in the shadow. He listened for any sound from the house, and his heart beat so heavily that he thought it must be heard in the silent garden.

Tonga crept across the roof beams and let himself down through the hole into Bartholomew's room, where the iron chest stood open on the table and the jewels glittered in the lamplight. Bartholomew, who was sitting beside it, looked up and saw the strange little figure standing in the middle of his floor, and he sprang to his feet with a cry. It was a cry, Small said afterwards, that cost the unfortunate man his life, and that none of them had ever meant to hear.

Tonga, who feared that the cry would bring the whole household running, flew into a sudden fierce rage and shot a poisoned dart from his blowpipe. Bartholomew fell back into his chair with that dreadful grin upon his face, and he never moved again. Small swore that he had never wished the man any harm, but Tonga, he said, had a nature as wild as the jungle where he was born.

Before he left, Tonga laid a paper bearing the four words of the old pledge beside the dead man, as Small had told him, so that the world might know whose hand had done it. Then he tied the iron box to the rope and lowered it into the garden, and slid down himself after it, as nimbly as a squirrel. In a moment the two of them were gone, with the heavy chest between them, and the garden was silent again.

Small and Tonga carried the chest to the Aurora, a fast launch that Small had hired from Mordecai Smith for the work, and they steamed away down the river and hid in a small boatyard on the south bank. Their plan was to wait there until the hunt had cooled and then to slip down to the sea and board a ship that would carry them to some far country. But Holmes's little army of street boys, as Small said with a bitter smile, had been too sharp for them.

Small said that when he saw the street boys hanging about the boatyard, he had guessed that the hunt was close, and he had made up his mind in an instant. If he could not have the treasure, nobody else should have it, and so, under cover of darkness, he had emptied the box into the river a handful at a time. It had cost him a leg and the best years of his life, he declared, and he had thrown the key in after the jewels, content to let the Thames keep them.

Small insisted that he had never meant any harm to Bartholomew Sholto, and that he grieved far more for the little islander who had given up his home and his people to follow him. Then he finished his story and sat back in silence, and Jones rose, laid a hand on his shoulder and led him away into the night. To the very last he declared that he had been robbed far more than he had ever robbed anyone, and that justice had never once been on his side.

When Watson told him of his engagement, Holmes congratulated him in his own dry fashion, though he remarked that love was an emotional thing. Whatever was emotional, he said, was opposed to the true cold reason which he placed above everything, and he would never marry himself, lest it should warp his judgement. Watson, who knew his friend well, thought that he sounded a little sad when he said it.

Inspector Jones took all the praise in the newspapers, and Holmes remarked wryly that Watson had won the lady and Jones the credit, and that for him there remained only the little bottle. Watson went out into the morning to his new life with Mary, as happy as a man could be, and Holmes stood alone at the window of Baker Street, watching the rain run down the glass. He knew that sooner or later another strange problem would walk through the door, and when it did, he would greet it like an old and welcome friend.
